TOKYO, Oct 30 : Japan's Panasonic Holdings said on Friday that operating profit at its energy unit surged to 55.6 billion yen ($352 million) in the second quarter from 1.2 billion yen a year earlier, boosted by higher sales of in-vehicle batteries and data centre energy storage systems. Here are more details: • Panasonic raised the unit's full-year profit forecast for the year ending March 2027 by 16 per cent to 198 billion yen from 171 billion yen previously. The company makes batteries for Tesla and other EV makers. • It also lifted its group operating profit forecast for the period by 120 billion yen, or 20 per cent, to 710 billion yen, in part due to stronger-than-expected growth in its AI-related businesses

Oct 30 : French IT consulting firm Capgemini raised its 2026 guidance for the second time this year after its third-quarter revenue grew 12 per cent, in the strongest signal yet that the rush to deploy AI is turning into contracts for Europe's established consultancies.  Capgemini CEO Aiman Ezzat said on Friday that third-quarter growth beat analyst expectations and outpaced the sector, with demand now concentrated in overhauling clients' data systems to adapt their business to AI. • Capgemini targets 2026 revenue growth of 9.0 per cent to 9.5 per cent at constant exchange rates, up from 8.5 per cent to 9.0 per cent previously • Third-quarter revenue rose to €6.07 billion ($6.78 billion), while bookings increased 3.4 per cent to €5.40 billion

FAST

Oct 30 : The Bank of Japan kept interest rates steady on Friday, but declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its price target and signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could be as soon as December. With underlying inflation roughly hitting the BOJ's 2 per cent target, the central bank must focus on anchoring it around that level, it said, stressing anew that its policy has entered a new, more hawkish phase open to raising rates once every few months. Following are excerpts from Governor Kazuo Ueda's comments at his post-meeting news conference, which was conducted in Japanese, as translated by Reuters: ON KEEPING RATES STEADY:

"We saw the need to scrutinise a bit more economic and price risks, as well as financial conditions. But underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with our price target. Financial conditions remain accommodative. There are various upside risks. We must therefore be vigilant to the risk of inflation overshooting our target." UNDERLYING INFLATION: "We will look at various indicators but more importantly, what kind of mechanism is behind price moves. We will focus particularly on whether medium- and long-term inflation expectations are anchored around our target." SUSTAINABLY ACHIEVING PRICE TARGET: "Our goal is to sustainably and stably achieve our price target. In that sense, we haven't reached our goal yet. It's important to anchor underlying inflation around our target. That doesn't mean we will just sit and wait. We will adjust monetary policy as appropriate so that underlying inflation becomes anchored around 2 per cent." UPSIDE RISKS: "There are still upside price risks we cannot ignore. But I won't say the risks have increased sharply from, say, one month ago." "It's true Japan's inflation expectations have yet to be anchored around our target. By taking appropriate monetary policy adjustments, we can make progress in achieving this particularly given upside price risks." LIKELIHOOD OF BASELINE SCENARIO: "We will look at the likelihood of our baseline scenario being achieved, as well as risks, at each policy meeting including at our next meeting." CUMULATIVE IMPACT OF RATE HIKES: "When our policy rate reaches levels deemed neutral to the economy, we can respond to both upside and downside risks. It's hard to judge when we can judge it as such. Among factors we will look at is the cumulative impact of our past interest rate hikes. That's why we must scrutinise financial conditions." PRICE PRESSURE BROADENING TO CONSUMERS: "Looking at various data, most of them were showing underlying inflation converging around 2 per cent ... We've already seen clear signs that rising energy and raw material costs from the Middle East conflict were pushing up business-to-business prices. Looking at September and October data, the upward pressure is now broadening to consumer price data. Such factors work to push up underlying inflation." ON FUTURE PACE OF RATE HIKES: "On the one hand, we will look at how big the risk of underlying inflation overshooting could be. On the other hand, we need to look at how accommodative financial conditions are. We must look comprehensively at such factors. The pace (of future rate hikes) will depend much on upcoming data. We can't decide in advance how many months we will spend each time before raising rates." UNDESIRABLE FOR INFLATION TO RISE SIGNIFICANTLY: "In the past, we could afford to allow underlying inflation to rise. With underlying inflation having reached 2 per cent, it's undesirable for inflation to rise significantly. That's why we must respond appropriately to upside price risks." ON FINANCIAL CONDITIONS: "We would like to adjust our policy rate as appropriate and bring financial conditions closer to neutral ... We need to cautiously look at financial conditions as what we see now may not necessarily fully reflect the cumulative impact of past rate moves." ON ACTING PRE-EMPTIVELY AND QUICKLY: "We're not there yet. We still need to work towards narrowing the gap between our policy rate and the neutral rate, and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation." ON WAGE NEGOTIATIONS "For underlying inflation to become anchored at 2 per cent, we need to see wage negotiations between firms and unions conducted on the assumption that inflation will move around 2 per cent. This year's consumer inflation may average 2 per cent or could be somewhat lower, so we need to see how this could affect next year's wage talks."

Source: Reuters

TOKYO : The Bank of Japan said on Friday it would sell about 860 billion yen (US$5.45 billion) in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) per year on a book value basis, accelerating the pace of sale. The central bank decided to sell its ETF holdings at a scale of about 0.1 per cent of trading value in the market, it said, as their value has been expanding in the stock market. It will now take about 43 years to complete the sales of its ETF holdings, versus the previously estimated 112 years, it said. The change will take effect from January 2027.

Source: Reuters

FAST

The Bank of Japan kept interest rates steady on Friday, but revised up its inflation forecast and stressed anew its readiness to continue pushing up borrowing costs to forestall mounting inflation risks. The central bank decided to maintain its short-term policy target at 1.25 per cent by an 8-1 vote. Board member Hajime Takata dissented to the decision. Governor Kazuo Ueda will hold a news conference at 3.30pm to explain the policy decision. COMMENTS

KAZUTAKA MAEDA, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MEIJI YASUDA RESEARCH INSTITUTE, TOKYO: "The outlook report suggests the BOJ has become more focused on upside risks to both inflation and economic activity as it struck a more upbeat tone on exports and capital spending driven by AI-related demand. "Although its inflation forecasts remain broadly consistent with the 2 per cent target, the BOJ seems increasingly conscious of the possibility that inflation could overshoot. "Rather than sticking to the previously assumed six-month interval between hikes, it may now be contemplating increases every three months, making the December meeting a credible opportunity for the next rate hike." DAVID CHAO, GLOBAL MARKET STRATEGIST FOR ASIA-PACIFIC, INVESCO, SINGAPORE: "My take-away from the initial report is the hawkish outlook on inflation, which sets the stage for a potential rate hike in December... all eyes will be on Ueda during this afternoon’s press briefing and whether he will tilt hawkish or dovish and any indication on how much higher rates can go. "The surprise news announcement is that the BOJ has decided to expedite its ETF sales, without trying to destabilise the market. While this may initially spook markets, I actually think this is a positive development since the BOJ feels confident enough with the economy and market." SHOKI OMORI, CHIEF JAPAN FIXED INCOME STRATEGIST, DEUTSCHE SECURITIES, TOKYO: "By judging that underlying inflation has reached 2 per cent, the BOJ has changed what it is trying to do: it is no longer a central bank trying to get to its target, it is one trying to keep inflation from running away from it. "That is a different reaction function, and the market should price in it as one. The 8-to-1 vote, with Takata calling for a hike, reinforces the point. "For rates, that shifts the debate from when the next hike comes to where the policy rate stops." MASATO KOIKE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, SOMPO INSTITUTE PLUS, TOKYO: "The ETF was the surprise. I was a little taken aback by that, but its weight is still small, so while it may have some impact on today's stock market, it is something that can be absorbed over the medium to long term without major disruption. "On prices, the BOJ's language that interest rates are broadly consistent with its outlook, together with the upgraded CPI forecasts in the Outlook Report, was largely as expected. But it allowed the BOJ to strengthen its rate-hike bias and hawkish stance more than before. "This can be taken as a signal toward a December rate hike, in the sense that the 2 per cent inflation target has been achieved. "The key points to watch in Ueda's news conference are his explanation on ETFs and his comments on the 2 per cent target." TOHRU SASAKI, CHIEF STRATEGIST, FUKUOKA FINANCIAL GROUP AND FORMER BOJ OFFICIAL, TOKYO: "Speeding up ETF sales is a bit surprising. It's unhealthy for the central bank to hold such a big amount of stocks, but I'm not sure if the timing was good in this risk-off environment. I'm a bit worried about the reaction in the Japanese stock market going forward. "Then in terms of monetary policy, the BOJ said that the underlying CPI inflation is at a level that is generally consistent with the price stability target of 2 per cent. They have been saying the underlying CPI is approaching the 2 per cent target. "So, the BOJ sounds a little bit soft, probably compared to the market expectation. In the end, this nuance of wording toward the underlying inflation and also just one dissident gives a somewhat less hawkish impression. "Probably Ueda-san will try to drive safely, especially in regard to the stock market reaction in the afternoon. So if the stock market decline is relatively large, Ueda-san cannot be so hawkish. His tone could be a bit dovish." HIROFUMI SUZUKI, CHIEF FX STRATEGIST, SMBC, TOKYO: "Board member Takata dissented, but this is unlikely to be a major market catalyst. The BOJ also announced a revision to the pace of its ETF sales. However, with the disposal of its ETF holdings still expected to take 43 years, the impact on financial markets is likely to be limited. "A significant shift from its previous assessments, however, was the BOJ's recognition that underlying inflation, excluding temporary factors, had reached its 2 per cent target. "Recent developments in France and declines in US equities have contributed to a tightening of global financial conditions. USD/JPY has also responded with yen appreciation at times, leaving the BOJ under no pressure to rush into a rate hike." MASAHIKO LOO, CHIEF FIXED INCOME STRATEGIST, STATE STREET INVESTMENT MANAGEMENT, TOKYO: "A boring hold, but an important shift in the Outlook Report. The BOJ's recognition that underlying inflation is now around 2 per cent brings its assessment closer to the reality that conventional inflation measures have already been around or above target for much of the past four years. "Taking its cue from the Fed and ECB, the BOJ has little reason to rush, particularly with US midterm elections potentially adding volatility across currencies and bonds. Ueda can stay data-dependent, keep every meeting live and preserve the next hike for around the turn of the year. "The surprise was the acceleration in ETF disposals. Cutting the estimated unwind from 112 years to 43 years is substantial, and at least puts completion within a human investment horizon. But 43 years is still extremely gradual, with annual sales amounting to only around 0.1 per cent of market turnover. The message is consistent with the broader normalization story: the BOJ is becoming more willing to unwind its legacy balance sheet, but remains determined to do so without disrupting markets."

Source: Reuters

HONG KONG, Oct 30 : The yen gained briefly after the Bank of Japan held rates but revised up an inflation forecast, while the dollar tracked Treasury yields lower as a fresh wave of selling in AI shares triggered a flight to safety. The BOJ left its main rate at 1.25 per cent in a widely anticipated move, but stressed that its policy has entered a new, more hawkish phase open to raising rates once every few months. The yen strengthened to a high of 157.115 per dollar, but later gave up those gains to trade steady at 157.67. It is on track to end October broadly flat. The brief nudge higher was due to the BOJ lifting its inflation forecast for the next financial year to 2.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent, as well as a dissenting opinion from one board member calling for a hike, said Shuhei Uehara, a foreign exchange analyst at Gaitame.com Research Institute.

The BOJ wraps up a week of central bank decisions, with the European Central Bank, the US Federal Reserve and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand all leaving interest rates unchanged as they bide their time amid stubborn inflation and tightening financial conditions.  But they are by no means done, with energy prices near multi-month highs and no resolution to the conflict in the Middle East in sight. The Bank of England and the Reserve Bank of Australia will be in focus next week, with investors watching their decisions. "I think this is just a temporary pause. The global tightening cycle is still going to continue and that will continue to be a driver for FX markets," said Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ. "The big question is as we enter 2027, whether or not we might end up with potentially even more hikes if the inflation stays elevated." The euro was flat at $1.1178 against the greenback after briefly dipping to its lowest since May 2025 in the previous session, and was on track for a 1.3 per cent monthly drop. Sterling strengthened 0.1 per cent to $1.3392, and was up 1 per cent for the month.  The Australian dollar was little changed at $0.7028, poised for a 1.2 per cent gain for October. The kiwi stood at $0.5634, flat for the month. NOT THE SAME AS AN ENERGY-DRIVEN RISK-OFF EPISODE The dollar index, which measures the US currency against a basket of peers, was a shade weaker at 101.85. It was set for a 0.3 per cent gain this month, marking a second straight monthly rise. The greenback was pulled lower by a dip in US Treasury yields as the safe-haven assets attract new bids. Results from Alphabet this week rekindled worries about AI spending, triggering a selloff in equities. The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note was last at 4.8958 per cent and that on the 30-year bond fell to 5.2623 per cent, both at their lowest in over a month. "The market reaction looked different from a conventional energy-driven risk-off episode," Sim Moh Siong, FX strategist at OCBC, said in a note. "Rather than supporting the USD and pushing US yields higher, US-centric AI concerns were accompanied by lower Treasury yields and a softer or broadly subdued USD."

TOKYO, Oct 30 : Annual core inflation in Japan's capital well exceeded the central bank's 2 per cent target in October, data showed on Friday, highlighting mounting price pressure and cementing the case for further interest rate hikes. The data came ahead of the Bank of Japan's policy announcement later on Friday. While the central bank is expected to keep policy steady, it is likely to stress its resolve to continue raising interest rates to prevent an inflation overshoot. The core consumer price index, which includes prices of fuel but not fresh food, in Tokyo rose 2.6 per cent in October from the same month a year earlier, government data showed, matching a median market forecast. It followed a 2.7 per cent rise in September. An index stripping away the effect of volatile fresh food and fuel prices, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a more accurate gauge of trend inflation, rose 2.6 per cent in October after a 2.9 per cent gain in September.

NEW YORK, Oct 29 : Wall Street's worries about the cost of the AI boom escalated after the market close on Thursday, as results from Amazon and Intel showed the infrastructure race is not only straining the tech industry but affecting consumers. Surging data-center spending, as highlighted in Amazon's massive cash burn, has turned once debt-light tech giants into major borrowers, while price hikes are squeezing global demand for devices like smartphones and PCs. Amazon forecast holiday-quarter sales below Wall Street expectations, a potential sign of growing pressure on consumers as inflation picks up, which also hit Intel's PC business, as a memory chip shortage has driven up its costs. The AI spending spree is also eating into Big Tech's once-enviable cash flows. Alphabet and Meta both burned cash in the September quarter, while Microsoft, the only exception, joined their borrowing binge with a $25 billion debt sale on Thursday.

The tech giants have deep pockets to sustain their spending, but investors have grown increasingly wary of smaller AI cloud firms borrowing heavily to deliver on enormous order backlogs. Amazon's 7 per cent after-hours slide was accompanied by losses of 5.8 per cent to 6.7 per cent in AI cloud stocks CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren. Alphabet, which closed regular trading down nearly 13 per cent, fell another 1.5 per cent after-hours. The semiconductor index also sold off post-close after Intel blamed "near term headwinds across the PC industry." The index had already dropped 1.4 per cent during the regular session due to Alphabet's messy earnings report.  Shares of PC makers HP and Dell sank 8 per cent and 6.8 per cent. "The revenues missed due to lower PC demand and forward guidance also disappointed. As Google learned today, earnings matter," said Kim Caughey Forrest, founder and chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners LLC. Google parent Alphabet dropped 13 per cent on Thursday. INTEL FACTORY SHUTDOWN Intel, whose shares were down 18 per cent, also said a factory explosion in Israel caused a two-week shutdown and would cost it roughly $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters.  "Overall semiconductor weakness after hours is primarily a function of Intel guide and negative sentiment spillover," said Michael James, equity sales trader at Rosenblatt Securities.  Some analysts said Intel's problems in the PC sector, an area of technology that does not garner the same scrutiny on Wall Street as the AI buildout, do not seem to necessarily mean big problems for other chipmakers that operate more prominently in AI. Nevertheless, investors in the less-active post-market trade chose to shoot first and ask questions later. AMD dropped 4 per cent and Broadcom fell 2 per cent. Among the biggest losers in the volatile session was the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull ETF, which offers investors three times the daily performance of the SOX and was off 9 per cent. The SOX has been one of 2026's standout performers, rising more than 60 per cent as shortages of chips and equipment needed for the AI buildout drive up prices and profits at firms ranging from giant Nvidia and memory chip firm Micron to Marvell Technology.  But the momentum of that trade has been tested over the past month by tightening financing terms. That has kept some expected IPOs on the sidelines and put some highly leveraged AI infrastructure firms under pressure. The SOX has declined 13 per cent since hitting its recent high in October and is off 21 per cent from its all-time high in June.  "I think Intel was seen as this unicorn within the tech sector because it was seen as being weaker compared to Nvidia and AMD," said Jake Dollarhide, chief executive officer of Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma.     "It just had this miraculous rise, and you got a lot of retail money into it, and some of that money is easy come, easy go."

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 30 : The Bank of Japan kept interest rates steady on Friday, but declared victory in a nearly 14-year battle to hit its price target and signalled vigilance against inflation risks, suggesting the next rate hike could be as soon as December. With underlying inflation roughly hitting the BOJ's 2 per cent target, the central bank must focus on anchoring it around that level, it said, stressing anew that its policy has entered a new, more hawkish phase open to raising rates once every few months. The broad shift in outlook aligns the BOJ with its US and European counterparts eyeing near-term rate hikes to battle inflationary risks from the AI boom and the Iran war-induced energy shock. In a surprise move that marks a further shift away from ultra-loose policy, the BOJ said it would accelerate its sales of exchange-traded funds from January to 860 billion yen ($5.45 billion) per year from 330 billion yen currently.

"Underlying inflation is at a level generally consistent with our price target, and is expected to remain at around that level," the BOJ said in a quarterly outlook report. "Against this backdrop, it will be important to examine the degree to which underlying inflation is anchored around 2 per cent." At the two-day meeting ending on Friday, the BOJ maintained its policy rate at 1.25 per cent in a widely expected move, forgoing back-to-back hikes to spend more time scrutinising the effects of past rate hikes on lending conditions. Hawkish board member Hajime Takata dissented to the decision to hold rates, instead proposing unsuccessfully a hike to 1.5 per cent. "We saw the need to scrutinise a bit more economic and price risks, as well as financial conditions. But underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with our price target," BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told a press conference after the decision. "Financial conditions remain accommodative. There are various upside risks. We must therefore be vigilant to the risk of inflation overshooting our target." TURNING POINT In the report, the BOJ revised up its core consumer inflation forecast for the fiscal year ending March 2028 to 2.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent projected three months ago. It upgraded its estimate for so-called "core core" inflation, which strips away the effect of fuel costs, for the next two fiscal years. The central bank also said long-term inflation expectations were "moving around 2 per cent," signalling its conviction sustained price and wage gains were becoming more embedded in the public's mindset. In the previous report released in July, the BOJ had said underlying inflation was nearing its 2 per cent target as long-term inflation expectations heightened gradually. "In the past, we needed to pay significant attention to downside price risks. We have seen a change in phase. From now on, we must focus on preventing the risk of underlying inflation overshooting our 2 per cent target from materialising," the report said. While the BOJ maintained its view financial conditions were accommodative, it said real interest rates were "rising recently, although those for short-term zones remain low." In the July report, it said real rates were "negative mainly in short- to medium-term zones." Declaring victory on the 2 per cent inflation target marks a turning point for the BOJ, which has spent most of its history battling low or negative price growth since gaining legal independence from the government in 1998. Under former governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the BOJ deployed massive monetary stimulus in 2013 to pull Japan out of deflation and fire up inflation to the 2 per cent target. Even after ending its mix of unorthodox easing steps in 2024, the BOJ has trodden cautiously in raising rates on the view underlying inflation - or price moves excluding one-off factors and driven by domestic demand - remained below target. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised rates in September after delivering a hike in June - a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025. Most analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate to 1.5 per cent in December, followed by further hikes next year. Their terminal rate projection centres around 1.75 per cent to 2 per cent. Rising prices, however, could weigh on consumption as they prod Japanese households, many of whom have never experienced widespread price gains in their lifetime, to seek discounts. ($1 = 157.8500 yen)

REVENUE DIVERSIFICATION GAINS TRACTION Prediction markets emerged as another area of growth for Coinbase during the reported quarter, with revenue exceeding $200 million. Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas said prediction markets and derivatives together accounted for about 25 per cent of its total transaction revenue, while subscription and services revenue made up roughly 49 per cent of total net revenue. "We are seeing the investments that we've made over the past few years to really diversify our revenue, really come to our benefit," Haas said. Coinbase's prediction markets had become one of the fastest-growing products in the company's history, helping drive additional spot trading volume, Third Bridge analyst Jacob Zuller said. The expansion also reflects its strategy of diversifying revenue streams beyond its core transaction business, which remains heavily dependent on crypto-market activity. "They (Coinbase) also treat the category (prediction markets) as near-term revenue, with derivatives as the longer bet," said Colby Howard, president of Heron Events at Heron Intelligence. "They also see prediction markets as a way in, with traders who start making money moving up to the paid tier," Howard said. Total operating expenses in the third quarter fell about 17 per cent to $1.15 billion, compared with $1.39 billion in the prior year. The Wilmington, Delaware-based firm reported a profit of $718.7 million, or $2.51 per share, for the quarter ended September 30, compared with $432.6 million, or $1.50 per share, a year earlier.

Source: Reuters

Oct 29 : Walmart said on Thursday it had extended its agreement with AI robotics firm Symbotic, committing about $6 billion over several years to bring more automation capabilities to its distribution network. Symbotic has been helping Walmart automate its supply chain since 2017. Under the agreement, Symbotic will bring additional automation capabilities to 25 of Walmart's regional distribution centers in the US and support its supply chain capabilities globally. Walmart said the agreement aimed to support its e-commerce upstream inventory management, increase storage capacity and improve how products move through the supply chain. These capabilities will help Walmart offer customers a broader assortment, improve speed and provide more reliable replenishment across its network, the retailer said. Retailers are increasingly deploying chatbots, along with targeted promotions and loyalty programs to entice shoppers who often turn to AI for product recommendations.

Source: Reuters
